King Shi

Introduction

Singer-songwriter Lana Del Rey has released 9 studio albums over her illustrious career. In 2024, she was going to release her 10th, but that didn’t happen. It was pushed back to be released on May 21, 2025. It’s now June 2025 and still no album (Paul 2025). While we sit back and patiently wait for it, let’s see if we can discern anything about this album by looking back at her past albums. Can we track the emotional and thematic evolutions throughout her albums, and potentially make some fun predictions about her new music using coding tools?

Lana’s Style

Lana is known for her storytelling, reaching the depths of human emotions, covering themes from love, heartbreak, grief, and identity (Jogezai 2023). Her earlier work heavily references the Americana aesthetic, both glamourising and critiquing it. One Medium user discusses how her music aided them with transformation and self-discovery, noting themes of “delusion and fantasy”, and Del Rey’s capacity to generate an atmosphere to romanticise reality. I tend to agree with these sentiments; for me, I find myself listening to her ethereal tunes when I’m feeling down. She often plays with irony and personas, particularly around American culture.

Her genre is generally labelled as alt-indie pop, but in 2024, Lana said about her new album:

“We’re going country. It’s happening” (Maher 2024).

So we have an indication. But that was before she delayed the rollout. Twice. Can we see patterns from her past music to hypothetically know what we’re going to get from the new album?

Genius Lyrics

There was a dataset of her entire discography uploaded to Kaggle (last updated July 2024), extracted from Genius.com. They note that the accuracy of the data is up to Genius’ discretion. Looking into how lyrics are added on Genius, we see that it’s a crowdsourced website. The more you contribute, the more access to editing power. The higher-profile an artist is, the harder it is to alter information on their pages. For an artist as popular as Lana Del Rey, there’s a lot of eyes on the lyrics, so most of her songs are either verified or pretty close to what she actually sings. That said, it’s still not perfect. There’s a big difference between how something is sung compared to what was sung.

On top of the limits to the dataset, there are some limits to the tools because they are analytical. As Rockwell and Sinclair (2016) remind us:

“Computers do not read meaning in a string. They process a sequence of characters” [p.28].

These computers cannot capture all the nuances of emotions, especially in music with things like tone, delivery, the atmosphere that create emotional responses. It can’t experience the beauty of listening to Summertime Sadness for the first time. So when we take these lyrics as plain text, even if they are accurate, they might get lost in translation.

Another broader discussion that Tenen (2016) brings up is digital tools “can discourage critical engagement with methodology” [p. 83], if we take them at face value. We must understand what the tools are doing and what they’re leaving out. Tenen (2016) continues:

“Some tools encourage intellectual laziness by obscuring methodology” [p. 85].

I need to know what my tools can and can’t tell us about Lana’s discography. While this dataset does give us Lana Del Rey’s lyrics, they’ve been filtered numerous times, by contributors, platform rules, the person who scraped the data, which all could potentially alter meanings. And the tools as well might have their own biases. But as long as we keep that in mind, this dataset should give us a solid enough base to explore emotion in linguistic contexts, and in particular Lana Del Rey’s powerful songwriting to maybe see where her sounds goes next.

Methods

Before I could analyse her music, I need to clean and restructure the data to what I need to do the things I want to do since I didn’t create the dataset. We’re going to do some sentiment analysis and topic modelling using some tools including NLTK, VADER, and scikit-learn.

Sentiment Analysis

To analyse sentiments over her music, VADER is appropriate for this project, which is a rule-based sentiment analysis tool optimised for social media (Hutto and Gilbert 2014). VADER scores each sentence on polarity (positive, negative or neutral) and intensity (compound), and accounts for capitalisation, punctuation, negation, and modifiers. Although lyrics on a page might convey different emotions to actually listening to Del Rey’s songs, we can use this tool to focus on her evocative lyricism, and see whether that’s changed over time. Some other limits noted by Franta and Silver (2024) is that sentiment analysis “falters when it comes to the sorts of rhetorically complex situations that populate literary prose” [p.403], which is prevalent in Lana’s music. Irony and sarcasm are some of the things that might be hard for a tool to decipher. This comes down to the complexity of human emotions, where a sentence can be interpreted so many different ways by different people. What’s useful about this tool is that it can follow a formula when interpreting sentiments to give one numerical score, rather than overthinking what the lyric is saying, even though humans might not agree with the output. Franta and Silver (2024) also describe “scale-free reading” [p. 404], which is the idea that sentiment analysis can be used for broad patterns or individual phrases, so looking at the emotional journey throughout albums or even her entire career. We can get a sense of how the emotional tone has shifted over time, but perhaps not what songs actually mean.

scikit-learn

To look at the themes across Lana’s albums, I used Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) from scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). LDA is a good for analysing lyrics because songs often contain overlapping themes, and since LDA treats each document as a blend of topics, it will be appropriate. CountVectorizer was used to vectorize lyrics, with stop word filtering, making a sparse document-term matrix for topic modelling. As Pedregosa et al. (2011) note, ’Scikit-learn exposes a wide variety of machine learning algorithms[…] using a consistent, task-oriented interface,” [p. 2829], making it handy for topic modelling in this musical analysis. Then, we can train LDA models with however many topics and then evaluate the top words in each topic to see what theme they might represent. In LDA, “each item of a collection is modeled as a finite mixture over an underlying set of topics” (Blei, Ng, and Jordan 2003, 993), meaning it doesn’t care about word order, it just looks at what words occur with each other.

Bringing it back to Rockwell and Sinclair (2016)’s point, computers are just grouping words that are near each other, they don’t actually know what they mean or the contexts. They can return topic clusters, but there still needs to be a human to interpret the outputs. Rockwell and Sinclair (2016) also says “formalization, not quantification, is the foundation of computer-assisted interpretation” [p. 41]. This is a good summation of the project. It’s not reducing the music into numbers, but finding patterns in the music for a human to pass judgement.

The Dataset!

The creator of the dataset notes that “This dataset prioritizes song coverage over album coverage; this means that deluxe versions of albums with more songs are chosen over standard versions, and that album releases are chosen over single/EP releases.” Meaning, there shouldn’t be any double-ups. Each album is listed in chronological order, and the songs are in album order.

Data Cleaning

There’s a lot of information provided, including non-album song, songs by others that Lana features on, officially released covers by Lana and so on. As the data was scraped from Genius, it also has other information like writers, producers, page views - stuff we don’t really need for our research (sorry!).

First, we get rid of anything between [square brackets] up to 100 characters. This was to make sure all the non-lyrics could be deleted, like [chorus] or [feature artists], without deleting the entire lyrics because they are lists enclosed in square brackets. There are no songs less than 100 characters, which is why 100 was the upper limit.

Code 
def remove_x(data,thing):
    data["song_lyrics"] = data["song_lyrics"].astype(str).apply(lambda x: re.sub(thing,"",x)).reset_index(drop=True)
    return data
Code 
remove_x(ldr_dataset,r'\[[^\[\]]{1,100}\]')

Next, we’ll remove stuff from the dataset we don’t want.

Code 
def remove_stuff(data_frame,category,thing):
    index = data_frame[data_frame[category].isin(thing)].index
    data_frame = data_frame.drop(index)
    return data_frame

Getting rid of “Non-Album Songs” and “Other Artist Songs” under the category column, and her EP Paradise and audiobook Violet Bent Backwards Over the Grass which are also included as their own category. One extra song included is hope is a dangerous thing for a woman like me to have - but i have it (Extended Version), under Norman Fucking Rockwell!. The extended version was released only on physical copies, and not found on Spotify. The lyrics are the same apart from a spoken outro by her producer. We’ll remove by number of page views, because it’s a unique number.

130 rows × 4 columns

Now to explode the song lyrics. The dataset puts each songs’ lyrics into a list, separating each line into strings with a comma in between. We can split each line at these commas, but only if it comes after a ’ or “, because there are some commas in the lyrics, and we don’t want to split them there.

Code 
def explode_lyrics(data):
    split_sentences = data[columns].copy()
    split_sentences["song_lyrics"] = (split_sentences["song_lyrics"].str.split(r'(?<=[\'"]),')
    )
    exploded_lyrics = split_sentences.explode("song_lyrics")
    exploded_lyrics = exploded_lyrics.reset_index(names="song_index")
    return exploded_lyrics
Code 
ldr_exploded_lyrics = explode_lyrics(cleanest_ldr_data)

def create_sentiment_scores(data):
    analyzer = nltk.sentiment.vader.SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()
    sentiment_scores = data["song_lyrics"].progress_map(analyzer.polarity_scores)
    sentiment_scores_df = sentiment_scores.apply(pd.Series)
    return sentiment_scores_df

def back_into_df(data):
    df_with_scores = data.assign(**sentiment_scores)
    df_with_scores = df_with_scores.assign(sentence_index = df_with_scores.groupby("song_title").cumcount())
    df_with_scores = df_with_scores.assign(album_sentence_index = df_with_scores.groupby("album_title").cumcount())
    return df_with_scores

def album_sentiments(data,x,y):
    plot = so.Plot(data=data, x="album_sentence_index", y="compound")
    plot = plot.label(x=x,y=y)
    plot = plot.add(so.Line())
    plot = plot.facet(col="album_title", wrap=5)
    plot = plot.share(x=False)
    plot = plot.layout(size=[16,6])
    return plot
Code

This shows the raw dynamics of Lana’s emotions over her albums. It’s very chaotic, so we can do a rolling mean of the lyrics to clear it up. I’ve picked the window half of the average of lines per song (around 25), to capture the emotional flow without smoothing it too much. Unfortunately it will cut the first and last 25 sentences, but it strikes a good balance between small enough to see the emotional shifts in the songs, but large enough to reduce the chaos from the graphs above.

Code 
avg_lines = lana_del_rey.groupby("song_title").size().mean()/2
Code 
def rolling_mean_album(data,x,y,window):
    compound_rollmean = (
        data              
        .groupby("album_title")              
        ["compound"]                    
        .rolling(window=window, center=True) 
        .mean()                        
        .droplevel("album_title")         
    )
    smoothed_scores = data.assign(compound_rollmean = compound_rollmean)
    plot = so.Plot(data=smoothed_scores, x="album_sentence_index", y="compound_rollmean")
    plot = plot.label(x=x,y=y)
    plot = plot.add(so.Line())
    plot = plot.facet(col="album_title", wrap=5)
    plot = plot.layout(size=[16,6])
    plot = plot.share(x=False)
    plot = plot.limit(y=[-1,1])
    return plot
Code 
rolling_mean_album = rolling_mean_album(lana_del_rey,"Lyric Position in Album","Rolling Mean Compound Score", int(avg_lines))
display(rolling_mean_album)

A limitation to note about taking the compounds is that a lot of the scores return a 0, meaning VADER likely couldn’t interpret it, or more unlikely it was a completely neutral lyric. We can simplify the sentiments by generating a polynomial curve fit to capture the overall emotional journey in an album with a single arc, so we can capture the general shifts within albums. For example, her second album Born to Die begins negatively, becomes more positive as the album progresses, then dips a little bit, but sort of plateaus and ends more positively than how she started.

Code 
def poly_fit(data,limit,x,y):
    plot = so.Plot(data=data, x="album_sentence_index", y="compound")
    plot = plot.label(x=x,y=y)
    plot = plot.add(so.Line(),so.PolyFit(order=3))
    plot = plot.facet(col="album_title", wrap=5)
    plot = plot.layout(size=[16,6])
    plot = plot.share(x=False)
    plot = plot.limit(y=limit)   
    return plot
Code 
poly = poly_fit(lana_del_rey,[-0.6,0.6],"Lyric Position in Album","Sentiment Scores (Compound)")
display(poly)

The overall arc can be graphed over all her released albums into a polynomial fit. While this downplays much of Lana’s artistry and emotion, it gives us a clear image of the general direction her career has gone in terms of lyrical emotional content.

Code 
    plot = so.Plot(data=lana_del_rey, x="index", y="compound")
    plot = plot.add(so.Line(),so.PolyFit(order=4))
    plot = plot.layout(size=[10,5])
    plot = plot.share(x=False)

We can deduce from the raw graph and rolling means graph the readings of emotions at a lyric level, albeit a bit messy. As we break down the data a bit more, we can examine more album wide sentiment structures. Lana Del Rey’s earlier albums showed more positive sentiment, followed by a subtle decline in lyrical tone over the years, with a slight upturn, before tailing off in her most recent albums.

But how do we interpret the scores about the lyrics? It differs from each researcher, so I followed (Bonta, Kumaresh, and Naulegari 2019, 4) and (Pano and Kashef 2020, 8) labelling anything above 0.05 as positive and below -0.05 as negative. Looking at the polyfit graph, it shows that most of Del Rey’s lyrics are positive, except for her last album, which dips just under 0.05, meaning it would be neutral.

I find this very interesting, because in my head Lana was always the representative of ‘sad girl’ music, so seeing this was surprising. That being said, I think it comes down to the atmosphere she is able to build with her sounds, how she sings and overall vibe, rather than her lyrics. I think this highlights the limits of computational tools sometimes and conflict with human interpretation.

Topic Modelling

I trialled with a different number of topics (5 to 10) and chose the one that returned the most meaningful and distinct groups. We don’t want too many topics, as (Blei, Ng, and Jordan 2003) note that as the number of topics increase, the model splits the words into smaller and smaller groups, which leads to harder interpretations of topics [p. 1011]. I decided to pick 5 topics to analyse to give a good balance between depth and readability. The goal is to generate interpretable clusters, because even if technically more topics produces more detailed outputs, the results will be less useful if they can’t be interpreted.

import matplotlib 
def plot_topic_composition_by_album(song_topic_df):
    """Show the mean probability for each topic for each newspaper in `document_topic_df` on a stacked
    bar chart."""

    tidy_data = song_topic_df.melt(
        id_vars=["index","album_title","song_title", "song_lyrics"], # keep
        var_name="topic", # new column for 'melted' column names
        value_name="probability" # new column for 'melted' cell values
    )

    # Defaults layer
    plot = so.Plot(tidy_data, x="album_title", y="probability", color="topic")
    
    # Element layer
    plot = plot.add(so.Bar(), so.Agg(), so.Stack()) 

    # Scales layer
    plot = plot.scale(x=so.Nominal())

    # Annotations layer
    plot = plot.layout(size=(16,8))

    # Label Layer
    plot = plot.label(title = "Probability of Song in Album to Belong to Topic", x = "Album Title", y = "Probability of Topic")
    return plot
Code 
def get_topic_word_matrix(topic_model, normalize=True):
    """Get the topic-word matrix for topic_model, with the word
    scores expressed as probabilities if `normalize` == True."""

    # Get pseudocounts
    topic_word_matrix = topic_model.components_

    # If desired, convert to probabilities
    if normalize == True:
        column_sums = topic_word_matrix.sum(
            axis=0,       # Sums of the columns
            keepdims=True # This is a numpy thing to make the division work - don't worry about it
        )
        topic_word_matrix = topic_word_matrix / column_sums
    
    return topic_word_matrix

def inspect_topic(topic_model, count_vectorizer, topic, n):
    """Return a data frame showing the top `n` words in `topic` in the passed
    `topic_model`, which used the passed `count_vectorizer` for text preprocessing."""

    topic_word_df = pd.DataFrame(
        data=get_topic_word_matrix(topic_model),
        columns=count_vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()
    )

    # START OF YOUR CODE
    topic_words = topic_word_df.sort_values(by=topic, ascending=False, axis=1)
    topic_words = topic_words.iloc[topic, :n] # 3 => row 3; :10 => first ten columns
    topic_words = pd.DataFrame(topic_words)
    topic_words = topic_words.reset_index(names=f" Topic {topic} Words")
    topic_words = topic_words.rename({topic: f"Topic {topic}"}, axis="columns")
    return topic_words
    # END OF YOUR CODE

In the graph, we can identify the probability a song within the albums to belong to which topic, and table shows us the chance the topic contains what certain word. Here are my interpretations:

  • Topic 0 - Americana/Religion: Reflects her references to American imagery, and some spiritually related words.
  • Topic 1 - Love/Desire/Fantasy: The first three words are interesting, but my guess is maybe onomatopoeias, or when someone is just mindlessly humming like dadadaaa. But words like lust, dreamin, bang, crimson reflects love, but with intensity and danger.
  • Topic 2 - Heartbreak/Emotional Distress: Emotionally charged words and motifs reflecting yearning and melancholia.
  • Topic 3 - Patriotism/Freedom/Identity: Similar to Topic 0, but with references to power in American culture, perhaps more critical. She plays some personas that reflect patriotism in an ironic way.
  • Topic 4 - Violence/Obsession: More narrative building around differrent characters. Could be linked to Topic 1. Yayo is slang for cocaine and reflections of drugs, violence, and addiction can be seen.

Her first two albums contain a lot of references to patriotic and darker, violent themes. There’s a rise in vulnerability and yearning as her career progresses, with more love and heartbreak. Since Chemtrails Over the Country Club, it seemingly returns to earlier themes, but maintains a steady level of wistfulness, but less mention of love/desire.

Conclusion: Album Prediction!

Bringing both the sentiment and topic analyses together, we observe a gradual decline in sentiment over her career. With the fading presence of love-related themes in her more recent albums, and return to darker narratives, my “super conclusive” prediction for her upcoming album leans into the negative tones and continues her return towards her storytelling of disillusioned patriotism and violence. With her claim of “going country”, a genre with tradional roots in Southern USA, a country album that is critical of Americanism, national identity would make sense for Lana Del Rey.
